summary: HTTP Origin-Bound Authentication (HOBA) is an experimental digital-signature-based design for an HTTP authentication method that can also be used in JavaScript-based login embedded in HTML. It is an alternative to schemes that require passwords.

eli5.summary: Instead of typing a secret password, your browser makes a special key for each website and proves it has it, like a signature only it can make.

questions: how does digital signature authentication work
subtitle: Digital-signature-based HTTP authentication that replaces passwords

tldr.problem: HTTP password-based authentication suffers from database breaches and phishing attacks. The server stores passwords, which attackers try to steal; users struggle to manage passwords across sites; and the protocol depends on secure transport but passwords are inherently at risk.
tldr.mechanism: HOBA creates a unique public-private key pair for each website a user visits. To log in, the browser receives a challenge from the server and signs it with the private key. The server verifies the signature and grants access. The keys are origin-bound, so a key for one website cannot be used for another.
tldr.outcome: Servers no longer store passwords, eliminating a major attack surface. The user's browser manages key pairs instead of the user managing passwords. It is experimental and has not achieved widespread adoption, but demonstrates a feasible alternative to password authentication for HTTP.

today: RFC 7486 is an Experimental protocol for HTTP authentication without passwords. While it demonstrates a viable alternative to password-based schemes, it has not achieved widespread adoption. The design remains relevant as an example of how cryptographic authentication can replace secrets stored on servers.

sections.title: Why Not Passwords?
sections.content:
HTTP Origin-Bound Authentication (HOBA) is a challenge-response authentication scheme that uses digital signatures in place of passwords. Instead of the server storing a password and the client proving it knows the password, the client proves it possesses a private key by signing a challenge sent by the server.

The core insight is that password databases are attack targets. When a server stores millions of password hashes, attackers try to breach the server to steal them, using tools like rainbow tables to crack weak hashes. HOBA avoids this entirely: the server never stores a shared secret, only the public key corresponding to each user's private key.

Each key pair is origin-bound, tied to a specific website. The browser generates a new key pair for each web origin (domain + port), so a compromised key for one site cannot be reused for another. Users no longer need to remember passwords or worry about reuse across sites.
sections.eli5: Passwords stored on servers can be stolen. Instead, your browser keeps a secret key just for that website. When the website wants to prove you're real, it asks you to sign something with your secret key. The website never learns the secret—it only checks that your signature is real.

sections.title: The HOBA Authentication Process
sections.content:
HOBA authentication happens in three phases:

1. Key Preparation: The browser checks if it has a Client Public Key (CPK) for the web origin the user is visiting. If not, it generates a new public-private key pair and stores it locally (in browser localStorage or similar). The CPK is a bare public key—no X.509 certificate overhead—and includes an algorithm identifier and a key identifier (kid).

2. Signing: The server sends a 401 (Unauthorized) response with a WWW-Authenticate header containing a challenge (a random base64url string) and a max-age (how long the challenge remains valid, e.g., 10 seconds). The browser constructs a HOBA-to-be-signed (HOBA-TBS) string containing the challenge, the origin (scheme://host:port), an optional realm, a nonce, and the algorithm identifier. It signs this string with the private key using the specified algorithm (e.g., RSA-SHA256).

3. Authentication: The browser sends back the signature and related fields in an Authorization header with the form Authorization: HOBA result=kid.challenge.nonce.sig. The server verifies the signature using the stored public key, checks that the origin and realm match, and if valid, creates a session (via a session cookie) so the user does not need to sign every request.
sections.eli5: Three steps: First, the browser makes a key pair if it doesn't have one. Second, when the website asks "prove you're you", the browser signs the challenge. Third, the website checks the signature and says "yes, you're logged in."

sections.title: Registration, Multiple Devices, and Logout
sections.content:
Registration: When a new user encounters a HOBA challenge for the first time, the browser generates a key pair and the server's registration process begins. The server can require confirmation (email, SMS, CAPTCHA) and optionally bind the CPK to an account name. Registration policy is entirely server-defined; HOBA does not mandate a particular flow.

Multiple Devices: A user may use multiple browsers or devices to access the same website. Each browser generates its own key pair. When a user logs in on a new device, the server can recognize this is a new CPK and ask the user to confirm their identity (via out-of-band methods like email), then associate the new CPK with the existing account. This avoids forcing users to register separately on each device.

Logout: Since HOBA uses session cookies for ongoing access, logout is straightforward: the client or server invalidates the session cookie, the same way as with password authentication.

Challenge Refresh: Because signatures take time to compute, the browser can prefetch a new challenge from the server before the current one expires, allowing it to pre-sign and reduce user-visible latency on the next request.
sections.eli5: New users can register on the website. If you use a different device, you can add its key to your account with a confirmation email. When you're done, just log out like normal.

sections.title: HOBA-http and HOBA-js
sections.content:
HOBA-http is the HTTP authentication scheme variant, using the standard WWW-Authenticate and Authorization headers. Servers check the signature and can reject a 401 response if validation fails. The signing process is deterministic and server-side validation is simple—any web server or application framework can implement it.

HOBA-js is a JavaScript design pattern for the same authentication concept, implemented entirely in client-side JavaScript without requiring browser support for a new HTTP scheme. It uses browser APIs like WebCrypto (if available) or JavaScript crypto libraries to sign, and localStorage (or IndexedDB) to store key pairs. The same HOBA-TBS format and signature algorithm apply. A server can offer both variants, falling back to JavaScript if the browser does not support HOBA-http natively.

For HOBA-js, there are additional security considerations: localStorage security relies on the browser's same-origin policy. Subdomains do not share localStorage by default, which can complicate enrollment for large sites; one solution is to use session cookies after logging in via HOBA on a main domain.
sections.eli5: HOBA can work two ways: as a new HTTP authentication scheme (if browsers support it), or as a JavaScript program embedded in web pages. Both use the same digital signature idea.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
No Password Database: The most significant security benefit is the absence of a stored password database. Servers store only public keys and account metadata. A breach of the server database does not compromise user credentials, though the public key itself (which is safe to leak) and associated metadata might be exposed.

Signature-Based Proof: The signature is a cryptographic proof of private key possession. Replay attacks are mitigated by the max-age parameter: signatures are only valid within the server-specified window (e.g., 10 seconds). Outside this window, the attacker must obtain a new challenge and re-sign.

Origin Binding: Keys are bound to a specific origin (scheme, host, port). The server MUST verify that the origin in the HOBA-TBS matches the request URL and the server's certificate. An attacker cannot use a key stolen from one site to authenticate to another.

Transport Security: All HOBA interactions require TLS to prevent interception. The client's private key is never exposed on the wire; only the signature is transmitted.

Privacy Concerns: The CPK is not publicly identified with the user's name or email (it is just a base64url-encoded key and identifier). However, if a user's CPK is tracked across sessions, it could be used as a unique fingerprint. Servers can mitigate this by using session cookies after successful authentication, so repeated requests do not include the CPK.
sections.eli5: No stolen database of passwords. Signatures only work during a short time window the server picks. Your key only works for one website, not others. Everything is encrypted. The server can't identify you just by looking at your key.
